issues.legal_issue: The State Legislature had competence to enact a law transferring rights in property to the State.
material_facts: The State Legislature enacted amendments transferring the right to hold certain fairs from former proprietors and tenure-holders to the State.
The amendments concerned the acquisition of property.
issues.conclusion: The amending legislation was within the State Legislature’s legislative competence under Article 246.
issues.legal_principle: Article 246, read with Entry 42 of the Concurrent List as amended by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, authorised legislation concerning the acquisition of property. The Court held that the amended legislative allocation permitted a State Legislature to enact an acquisition law even without a public purpose, subject to the separate restriction in Article 31(2).

rule.if: legislative_competence_challenge and state_legislature_enacted_law and law_concerns_property_acquisition and constitutional_allocation_authorizes_state_acquisition_laws

predicates.legislative_competence_challenge: A proceeding challenges whether a State Legislature had authority to enact the law.
predicates.state_legislature_enacted_law: A State Legislature enacted the law under challenge.
predicates.law_concerns_property_acquisition: The law provides for the transfer or acquisition of property rights by the State.
predicates.constitutional_allocation_authorizes_sta: The constitutional allocation of legislative powers authorises the State Legislature to enact laws concerning property acquisition.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges legislative competence, a State Legislature’s law concerning property acquisition is within its competence if the constitutional allocation authorises the State Legislature to enact such laws.

issues.legal_issue: A law acquiring rights in an estate is protected from invalidation for inconsistency with fundamental rights when it falls within the constitutional protection for estate acquisition.
material_facts: The amendments retrospectively transferred to the State the right to hold fairs on specified lands.
The right to hold a fair on one’s land was treated as a mode of using the land and as an interest in land.

The amendment’s retrospective operation meant that the relevant rights could be treated as rights of intermediaries at the effective time; alternatively, the constitutional definition of rights in relation to an estate included rights of raiyats.
The relevant estates continued to fall within the applicable definition of an estate.
issues.conclusion: The amending legislation provided for the State’s acquisition of rights in an estate and was not void on the ground that it violated Articles 14, 19 or 31.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A provides that a law providing for the State’s acquisition of an estate or rights in an estate is not void because it is inconsistent with, takes away or abridges rights under Articles 14, 19 or 31. Article 31A(2)(b), as amended by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, includes rights of raiyats and under-raiyats; the words “or other intermediary” do not restrict those expressly included categories. A right to hold a fair on land is an interest in that land. The Court also relied on the retrospective effect of the amendments and the continued existence of the estates under the applicable definition.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A proceeding challenges the validity of a law on the ground that it infringes constitutional rights.
predicates.state_acquires_rights_in_an_estate: The law provides for the State to acquire rights associated with an estate.
predicates.acquired_right_is_an_interest_in_land: The right acquired by the State is an interest in land, such as a right to use land for a particular purpose.

issues.definition: If a constitutional validity challenge concerns a law by which the State acquires an interest in land associated with an estate, the law is not void for inconsistency with fundamental rights.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of a public purpose does not invalidate an acquisition law that is protected as a law acquiring rights in an estate.
material_facts: The amendments transferred to the State the right to hold fairs, a transfer that could augment State revenue.
The Court considered whether the acquisition could be invalid because it was not for a public purpose.
The Court determined that the acquisition fell within the constitutional protection for laws acquiring rights in an estate.
issues.conclusion: The law was not invalid merely because the acquisition was not for a public purpose.
issues.legal_principle: After the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, Article 31(2) expressly made public purpose a condition of compulsory acquisition, while Article 31A protected qualifying estate-acquisition laws from invalidation under Article 31. The Court held that Article 31A therefore covered an acquisition even if it was not for a public purpose. It considered The State of Bihar v. Sir Kameshwar Singh, [1952] S.C.R. 880, and held that the later constitutional amendments had removed the basis for the earlier argument that public purpose could be judicially required in this context. The Court also relied on Entry 42 of the Concurrent List as amended by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A proceeding challenges the validity of an acquisition law.
predicates.acquisition_lacks_public_purpose: The acquisition is not for a public purpose.
predicates.acquisition_is_protected_estate_acquisit: The acquisition is of rights in an estate and falls within the constitutional protection for estate-acquisition laws.

issues.definition: If a constitutional validity challenge concerns an acquisition without a public purpose that is protected as an acquisition of rights in an estate, the law is not invalid solely for lacking a public purpose.
